reply_text:
Timing each futon1b read the agreement route makes, to see which one takes the 11 seconds.I found the cause of the 11 seconds and am checking one detail in futon1b before I report.I'm changing the Emacs acceptance check so it no longer blocks Emacs while it waits, then I'll test it against the live server.The background call works: it returned the agreement for your yes and refused the agent-turn evidence, each in the right buffer. One last tidy-up, then I'll commit.There's an Emacs test file for this code that I'd missed; running it now.All 53 tests pass, and the updated test fails against the old code. I'm adding one test that the turn goes out before the answer arrives.㊥ Gist: Recording a yes no longer blocks Emacs. The request now runs in the background, and the "yes: agreement …" line appears in your buffer when the server answers. That's loaded in your Emacs and committed. The 11 seconds came from futon1b. Two of the agreement route's reads normally take a few milliseconds, but took 6.5 and 7.3 seconds while it was busy with other reads at the start of your turn. I haven't found why those reads slowed down.

㊢ (what the log shows) This is futon1b's journal for the 18 seconds after your "🈸:yes 1" at 14:02:13:
- **Evidence:** your turn's evidence was written and read back in under 50 ms.
- **The slow reads:** the list of this session's offers took 6,533 ms. Then the list of agreements on an older offer of mine took 7,299 ms. Run now, both take about 0.5 ms.
- **What ran at the same time:** the reads for the pattern card shown in your prompt line, each about 2.7 s. These are queries for the state at a given moment, and the moment changes every turn, so they're never cached. Evidence writes were also going on.
- **The result:** the agreement was written at 14:02:27 by your own request. The server kept going after Emacs gave up at 3 s.

㊟ (what I couldn't pin down) It isn't futon1b's limit on concurrent heavy reads: that allows 4, and at most 3 were held. I ran one uncached pattern-card read alongside an offer read, and the offer read still took 3 ms. So the slowdown needs more than one competing read, or something else that was happening at 14:02. Finding it is futon1b work: reproduce several uncached reads at once, the way a turn start does.

㊢ (the Emacs change, commits 53dbffd2, 6fdced7f, d63d2647)
- **Background request:** `agent-chat--agreement-post-async` sends the agreement in the background, with a 60 s deadline. The outcome line goes to the buffer that asked, even if you've moved to another buffer by then.
- **Clearer refusals:** a refusal now gives its reason, e.g. "http 403, evidence-not-operator-turn".
- **Agent timing:** the agent still gets the turn immediately. If the server is slow, the agent sees the agreement in the next turn's header, as happened this turn.

㊬ (what I checked)
- **Live, in your Emacs:** I fired your real yes and an agent turn's evidence at the server. The first came back 200 with agreement `act:e77e3e43…` (the existing one, not a duplicate). The second came back 403, each to its own buffer.
- **Tests:** the agent-chat ERT tests pass, 54 of 54. I had missed that they called the old synchronous request function, so I updated them. The new test checks that the turn is sent before the answer arrives and that the line lands in the right buffer. Both the updated test and the new one fail against the old blocking code.
- **Not run:** the rest of the Emacs test files.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(what happened)
- **The failure:** I sent the same request by hand with your turn's evidence id (`emacs-bb6cccc9…`), and it took 11.4 s to return the agreement. `agent-chat-agreement-timeout` is 3 s. Emacs gave up and printed the status as 0.
- **What was recorded:** the agreement's timestamp is 14:02:27, fourteen seconds after your turn at 14:02:13. So most likely your own request finished on the server after Emacs stopped waiting, and my call got that same record back. Agreements are keyed by offer, option and evidence, so a repeat returns the existing one rather than adding another. I haven't confirmed which call wrote it, but either way there is one agreement, not two.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (why it matters) A yes that is recorded while the buffer says "not checked" looks like a failure when it isn't. If you then retype it, the repeat is harmless, but the buffer gives you the wrong information.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(fixes, in order of size)
1. **Make the Emacs call asynchronous.** Post the agreement in the background and insert the "yes: agreement …" line when it returns. Simply raising the timeout would freeze Emacs for 11 seconds on every yes.
2. **Find the slow step.** The route is fast when it refuses (under 0.1 s), so the time is probably spent on the futon1b reads and writes it makes when it succeeds. That needs measuring before it can be fixed.
